notes:
Sign convention (Cartesian)

Distances measured from the pole/optical centre; along incident light positive. Real object: $u$ negative. Concave mirror / convex lens: $f$ negative / positive respectively.

Mirrors

  • $\dfrac1v + \dfrac1u = \dfrac1f$, $f = R/2$, magnification $m = -\dfrac{v}{u}$.
  • Concave mirror: object beyond $C$ → image between $F$ and $C$, real, inverted, diminished; between $F$ and $P$ → virtual, erect, magnified. Convex mirror: always virtual, erect, diminished.

Refraction

  • Snell's law $n_1\sin i = n_2\sin r$; $n = c/v = \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}$.
  • Critical angle: $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{n}$ (denser to rarer). TIR needs denser → rarer and $i > C$. Diamond ($n=2.42$, $C \approx 24^\circ$), optical fibre, mirage, prism binoculars.
  • Glass slab: emergent ray parallel to incident; lateral shift $= \dfrac{t\sin(i-r)}{\cos r}$.
  • Spherical surface: $\dfrac{n_2}{v} - \dfrac{n_1}{u} = \dfrac{n_2 - n_1}{R}$.

Lenses

  • $\dfrac1v - \dfrac1u = \dfrac1f$, $m = \dfrac{v}{u}$, power $P = \dfrac{1}{f(\text{m})}$ dioptre.
  • Lens maker: $\dfrac1f = (n_{rel} - 1)\left(\dfrac1{R_1} - \dfrac1{R_2}\right)$. In a medium with $n_m$, use $n_{rel} = n_g/n_m$ → focal length increases in water; lens becomes diverging if $n_m > n_g$.
  • Lenses in contact: $P = P_1 + P_2$, $\dfrac1F = \dfrac1{f_1} + \dfrac1{f_2}$.
  • Object at $2f$ gives real image of same size at $2f$. Minimum distance between real object and real image $= 4f$.

Prism

  • $i + e = A + \delta$; at minimum deviation $n = \dfrac{\sin\frac{A+\delta_m}{2}}{\sin\frac A2}$. Thin prism: $\delta = (n-1)A$.
  • Dispersion: violet deviates most ($n_v > n_r$). Rainbow = refraction + dispersion + TIR.

Optical instruments

  • Simple microscope: $m = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f}$ (image at $D = 25$ cm), $m = \dfrac{D}{f}$ (image at infinity).
  • Compound microscope: $m = \dfrac{L}{f_o}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)$ approximately; $f_o$ small, $f_e$ small.
  • Telescope (normal adjustment): $m = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e}$, length $= f_o + f_e$; $f_o$ large, $f_e$ small. Reflecting telescope: no chromatic aberration, brighter.

Exam tip

3–4 questions every year. Do mirror/lens formula numericals with signs carefully; memorise prism formula and telescope/microscope magnification.

questions.q: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. The image is formed at
questions.explanation: $\dfrac1v = \dfrac1f - \dfrac1u = -\dfrac1{10} + \dfrac1{15} = -\dfrac1{30}$ → $v = -30$ cm: real, inverted, magnified ($m = -2$).
questions.trick: Mirror: $1/v=1/f-1/u$; use sign convention (concave $f$ negative, real $u$ negative).

questions.q: The refractive index of a medium is $\sqrt2$. Its critical angle is
questions.explanation: $\sin C = 1/n = 1/\sqrt2 \Rightarrow C = 45^\circ$.
questions.trick: $\sin C=1/n$ — plug in $n$, solve the inverse sine directly.

questions.q: A lens has a focal length of $-25$ cm. Its power is
questions.explanation: $P = 1/f(\text{m}) = 1/(-0.25) = -4$ D. Negative → concave (diverging) lens.
questions.trick: $P=1/f(\text{m})$; the sign of $f$ gives the sign of power directly.

questions.q: Two thin lenses of powers $+5$ D and $-2$ D are placed in contact. The focal length of the combination is
questions.explanation: $P = 5 - 2 = 3$ D → $f = 1/3$ m $= 33.3$ cm, converging.
questions.trick: Lenses in contact: powers simply add, $P=P_1+P_2$.

questions.q: For a prism of angle $60^\circ$, the angle of minimum deviation is $30^\circ$. The refractive index of the prism material is
questions.explanation: $n = \dfrac{\sin\frac{A+\delta_m}{2}}{\sin\frac A2} = \dfrac{\sin45^\circ}{\sin30^\circ} = \dfrac{1/\sqrt2}{1/2} = \sqrt2$.
questions.trick: Prism: $n=\sin\frac{A+\delta_m}{2}/\sin\frac{A}{2}$ — the half-angle formula, memorise it.

questions.q: The magnifying power of a simple microscope of focal length 5 cm, when the image is formed at the near point (25 cm), is
questions.trick: Near-point viewing: $m=1+D/f$; at infinity drop the '+1'.

questions.q: An astronomical telescope has objective and eyepiece of focal lengths 100 cm and 5 cm. In normal adjustment its magnifying power and length are
questions.trick: Telescope: $m=f_o/f_e$, tube length $=f_o+f_e$ — two formulas, learn both.

questions.q: A convex lens of glass ($n = 1.5$) has focal length 20 cm in air. Its focal length in water ($n = 4/3$) is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{f_w}{f_a} = \dfrac{n_g - 1}{n_g/n_w - 1} = \dfrac{0.5}{1.125 - 1} = 4 \Rightarrow f_w = 80$ cm.
questions.tip: Focal length of a glass lens becomes about 4 times in water.
questions.trick: Lens in water: use $n_{rel}=n_g/n_m$ in the lens-maker equation; $f$ roughly quadruples.

questions.q: A convex lens forms a real image of the same size as the object. The object is placed at
questions.explanation: Object at $2f$ → image at $2f$ on the other side, real, inverted, same size ($m = -1$).
questions.trick: Object at $2f$ gives image at $2f$, same size, inverted — an instant recall pair.

questions.q: A swimming pool appears 3 m deep when viewed vertically from above. If the refractive index of water is $4/3$, the real depth is
questions.explanation: Real depth $= n\times$ apparent depth $= \dfrac43\times3 = 4$ m.
questions.trick: Real depth $=n\times$ apparent depth — denser medium looks shallower.

questions.q: Which colour of light undergoes the maximum deviation in a glass prism?
questions.explanation: Violet has the shortest wavelength and highest refractive index in glass, so it deviates most. $\delta = (n-1)A$.
questions.trick: Violet bends most: shortest $\lambda$ gives highest $n$ gives highest deviation.

questions.q: Total internal reflection occurs when light travels
options: from denser to rarer medium with angle of incidence less than the critical angle
from rarer to denser medium with angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
from rarer to denser medium at any angle
from denser to rarer medium with angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
questions.explanation: Both conditions are needed: denser → rarer and $i > C$.
questions.trick: TIR needs BOTH conditions: denser to rarer AND angle greater than critical angle.

questions.q: The image formed by a convex mirror is always
questions.explanation: Convex mirrors have a wide field of view and always form virtual, erect, diminished images — hence used as rear-view mirrors.
questions.trick: Convex mirror: always virtual, erect, diminished — no exceptions, ever.

questions.q: A ray of light passes through a glass slab. The emergent ray is
options: parallel to the incident ray but laterally shifted
questions.explanation: The two refractions at parallel faces cancel the deviation; only a lateral shift $t\sin(i-r)/\cos r$ remains.
questions.trick: Slab: net deviation is zero, only a lateral shift remains — no direction change.

questions.q: The minimum distance between a real object and its real image formed by a convex lens of focal length $f$ is
questions.explanation: With object at $2f$, image at $2f$: separation $4f$. For any other position the separation is larger.
questions.trick: Minimum real-object-to-real-image separation via a convex lens is always $4f$.

questions.q: A thin prism of angle $5^\circ$ made of glass ($n = 1.5$) produces a deviation of
questions.explanation: $\delta = (n - 1)A = 0.5\times5^\circ = 2.5^\circ$.
questions.trick: Thin prism: $\delta=(n-1)A$ — no need for the full sine formula.

questions.q: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 15 cm. The image formed is
options: 8.6 cm in front of the mirror, real and diminished
8.6 cm behind the mirror, virtual and diminished
34.3 cm behind the mirror, virtual and magnified
12 cm behind the mirror, virtual, same size
questions.explanation: $\dfrac1v=\dfrac1f-\dfrac1u=\dfrac1{15}-\dfrac1{-20}=\dfrac1{15}+\dfrac1{20}=\dfrac{7}{60}$, so $v\approx8.6$ cm (positive, behind the mirror); convex mirrors always give virtual, diminished images.
questions.trick: Convex mirror: $f$ and $v$ both positive → image always behind, virtual.

questions.q: A person suffering from myopia (short-sightedness) can see nearby objects clearly but not distant objects. This defect is corrected using a
questions.explanation: In myopia the image of a distant object forms in front of the retina; a diverging (concave) lens shifts it back onto the retina.
questions.trick: Myopia (far objects blurry) needs a concave lens; hypermetropia needs a convex lens.

questions.q: A hypermetropic eye has its near point at 50 cm instead of 25 cm. The power of the corrective lens needed so that an object at 25 cm forms a virtual image at 50 cm is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac1v-\dfrac1u=\dfrac1f$: with $u=-25$ cm, $v=-50$ cm, $\dfrac1f=-\dfrac1{50}+\dfrac1{25}=\dfrac1{50}$, so $f=50$ cm $=0.5$ m and $P=+2$ D.
questions.trick: Hypermetropia fix: apply $1/f=1/v-1/u$ with the given near points, then $P=1/f$.

questions.q: Presbyopia (age-related loss of the eye's power of accommodation, causing the near point to recede) is corrected using
options: bifocal lenses combining convex and concave portions
questions.explanation: Presbyopia often accompanies both near- and far-vision difficulty in the same person, so bifocal lenses (convex portion for near vision, concave for distant vision) are used.
questions.trick: Presbyopia = both defects together → bifocal (convex+concave) lenses.

questions.q: A convex spherical surface of radius 20 cm separates air ($n=1$) from glass ($n=1.5$). An object is placed 100 cm from the surface in air. Using $\dfrac{n_2}{v}-\dfrac{n_1}{u}=\dfrac{n_2-n_1}{R}$, the image distance is
questions.trick: Curved surface: $n_2/v-n_1/u=(n_2-n_1)/R$ — plug in signs carefully.

questions.q: Two thin convex lenses, each of focal length 10 cm, are placed coaxially 5 cm apart. The equivalent focal length of the combination is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac1F=\dfrac1{f_1}+\dfrac1{f_2}-\dfrac{d}{f_1f_2}=0.1+0.1-\dfrac{5}{100}=0.15$, so $F\approx6.67$ cm.
questions.trick: Separated lenses: $1/F=1/f_1+1/f_2-d/(f_1f_2)$ — subtract the extra term.

questions.q: A plano-convex lens of focal length 20 cm has its plane surface silvered. It now behaves like a mirror of focal length
questions.explanation: For a lens silvered on one face, equivalent power $P_{eq}=2P_{lens}+P_{mirror}$. With the plane face silvered ($P_{mirror}=0$), $P_{eq}=2/20=0.1$, giving $f_{eq}=10$ cm, behaving as a converging (concave-type) mirror.
questions.trick: Silvered lens acts as a mirror: $P_{eq}=2P_{lens}+P_{mirror}$.

questions.q: The resolving power of a microscope is higher when
options: the objective lens diameter is reduced
a shorter wavelength of light and a larger numerical aperture are used
a longer wavelength of light is used
questions.explanation: Resolving power $\propto \dfrac{2n\sin\theta}{\lambda}$ (numerical aperture over wavelength); using shorter-wavelength light and a larger aperture angle improves resolution.
questions.trick: Resolving power is proportional to numerical aperture over $\lambda$ — shorter $\lambda$, bigger aperture wins.

questions.q: Chromatic aberration in a lens, caused by different colours having different focal lengths, is minimised by using
options: coating the lens with a reflective film
an achromatic doublet — a combination of convex and concave lenses of different materials
questions.explanation: An achromatic combination of a convergent and a divergent lens of different dispersive powers can bring two colours to the same focus, greatly reducing chromatic aberration.
questions.trick: Chromatic aberration fix = achromatic doublet (converging plus diverging, different $n$).

questions.q: Spherical aberration in a lens/mirror refers to the defect in which
options: different colours focus at different points
paraxial and marginal rays focus at different points, blurring the image
the image suffers from a lateral shift
questions.explanation: Rays striking near the edge (marginal rays) of a spherical lens/mirror focus at a different point than paraxial rays, causing a blurred image called spherical aberration; it can be reduced using a stop or parabolic mirrors.
questions.trick: Spherical aberration = marginal vs paraxial rays focus differently — use a stop.

questions.q: A convex lens of focal length 10 cm and dispersive power $\omega_1=0.02$ is to be combined with a second lens of dispersive power $\omega_2=0.03$ to form an achromatic combination. The focal length of the second lens must be
questions.explanation: Achromatism requires $\dfrac{\omega_1}{f_1}+\dfrac{\omega_2}{f_2}=0 \Rightarrow f_2=-\dfrac{\omega_2f_1}{\omega_1}=-\dfrac{0.03\times10}{0.02}=-15$ cm (a diverging lens).
questions.trick: Achromatism condition: $\omega_1/f_1+\omega_2/f_2=0$ — solve for the unknown $f$.

questions.q: The sky appears blue because
options: air molecules absorb all colours except blue
blue light travels faster than other colours in air
red light is scattered more than blue light
shorter wavelengths (blue) are scattered more strongly by air molecules than longer wavelengths (Rayleigh scattering, $\propto 1/\lambda^4$)
questions.explanation: Rayleigh scattering by air molecules is much stronger for shorter wavelengths, so blue light is scattered across the sky far more than red, giving the sky its blue colour.
questions.trick: Rayleigh scattering goes as $1/\lambda^4$ — blue scatters most, hence blue sky.

questions.q: The sun appears reddish at sunrise/sunset because
options: red light is absorbed by the atmosphere at sunset
the sun's temperature decreases at sunset
the eye's sensitivity to blue decreases at sunset
most of the blue light is scattered away by the longer path through the atmosphere, leaving mainly red light to reach the eye
questions.explanation: At sunrise/sunset, sunlight travels a much longer path through the atmosphere; the shorter (blue) wavelengths are scattered away en route, leaving the transmitted light dominated by red/orange.
questions.trick: Sunset: longer atmospheric path scatters away blue, leaving red to reach the eye.

questions.q: Optical fibres transmit light over long distances with very little loss using
options: total internal reflection at the core-cladding interface, since the core has a higher refractive index than the cladding
ordinary reflection from a silvered coating
questions.explanation: Light entering the fibre core (higher $n$) strikes the core-cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle and undergoes repeated total internal reflection, travelling with minimal loss.
questions.trick: Optical fibre works via TIR: core $n$ greater than cladding $n$, always.

questions.q: A mirage is formed on a hot road because
options: air near the ground is denser (higher $n$) than the air above it, bending light upward
water actually collects on the road surface
hot air near the ground has a lower refractive index than the cooler air above, causing rays from the sky to bend and undergo (near) total internal reflection, appearing as a reflection
light from the sky is reflected by a silvered layer of sand
questions.explanation: Hot air close to the road is less dense (lower $n$) than the cooler air above; light from the sky refracts continuously through these layers and eventually curves upward as if reflected, creating the illusion of a water pool.
questions.trick: Mirage: hot ground air has lower $n$ → light curves up, mimics reflection.

questions.q: The critical angle for light travelling from water ($n=4/3$) to air is
questions.explanation: $\sin C=1/n=3/4=0.75 \Rightarrow C\approx48.6^\circ$.
questions.trick: $\sin C=1/n$; for water $n=4/3$ gives $C\approx48.6°$ — a common one to memorise.

questions.q: A tank has a 6 cm layer of water ($n=4/3$) on top of a 4 cm layer of glass ($n=1.5$). Viewed from directly above, the apparent total depth of the two layers is
questions.explanation: For near-normal viewing, apparent depth of stacked layers $=\sum(t_i/n_i)=\dfrac{6}{4/3}+\dfrac{4}{1.5}=4.5+2.67\approx7.17$ cm.
questions.trick: Stacked layers: apparent depth $=\sum t_i/n_i$ — add each layer's own apparent depth.

questions.q: In the Cartesian sign convention used for mirrors and lenses, the object distance $u$ for a real object is always taken as
options: dependent on whether the mirror is concave or convex
negative, since it is measured against the direction of incident light
questions.explanation: With incident light taken as travelling in the positive direction, a real object (always in front of the mirror/lens) has $u$ measured backward from the pole/optical centre, so $u$ is negative.
questions.trick: Real object $u$ is always negative — incident light direction is the positive axis.

questions.q: A compound microscope has objective focal length 1 cm, eyepiece focal length 5 cm, a tube separation of 20 cm, and forms the final image at the near point (25 cm). Its magnifying power is approximately
questions.explanation: $m\approx\dfrac{L}{f_o}\left(1+\dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)=\dfrac{20}{1}\times\left(1+\dfrac{25}{5}\right)=20\times6=120$.
questions.trick: Compound scope: $m=(L/f_o)(1+D/f_e)$ — multiply the two magnification factors.

questions.q: In an astronomical telescope, decreasing the focal length of the eyepiece
options: has no effect on the magnifying power
increases the magnifying power but reduces the field of view
questions.explanation: $m=f_o/f_e$, so a smaller $f_e$ gives higher magnification, but this comes at the cost of a narrower field of view.
questions.trick: Smaller eyepiece $f_e$ gives more zoom but a narrower field of view — trade-off.

questions.q: A dentist uses a mirror that gives an erect, magnified virtual image of the teeth. This mirror is
options: concave, with the teeth placed beyond the centre of curvature
concave, with the teeth placed within its focal length
questions.explanation: A concave mirror with the object (teeth) placed between the pole and focus produces a virtual, erect, magnified image, ideal for close dental examination.
questions.trick: Concave mirror with object inside focus gives magnified virtual image (dentist's trick).

questions.q: A shaving/makeup mirror that produces an enlarged, erect image of the face held close to it is
options: a combination of two plane mirrors
questions.explanation: Held within its focal length, a concave mirror forms a magnified, erect, virtual image, which is why it is used for shaving and makeup.
questions.trick: Shaving/makeup mirror is concave, held within focal length for a magnified erect image.

questions.q: A biconvex lens has both faces of radius of curvature 10 cm and is made of glass with $n=1.5$. Its focal length is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac1f=(n-1)\left(\dfrac1{R_1}-\dfrac1{R_2}\right)=0.5\left(\dfrac1{10}-\dfrac1{-10}\right)=0.5\times0.2=0.1 \Rightarrow f=10$ cm.
questions.trick: Biconvex, equal radii: $1/f=(n-1)(2/R)$ — $R_1$ positive, $R_2$ negative, don't cancel.

questions.q: For a convex lens, when a real object is placed between $f$ and $2f$, the image formed is
questions.explanation: For an object between $f$ and $2f$, the convex lens forms a real, inverted image that is magnified and located beyond $2f$ on the other side.
questions.trick: Between $f$ and $2f$ gives an image beyond $2f$: real, inverted, magnified (projector case).

questions.q: For a given pair of media, the critical angle for total internal reflection is smallest for which colour of light, and why?
options: Violet, because it has the highest refractive index and hence the smallest critical angle
Red, because it has the highest refractive index
Green, because the critical angle does not depend on colour
Yellow, because it has the lowest refractive index
questions.explanation: Since $\sin C = 1/n$, a higher refractive index gives a smaller critical angle. Violet light has the shortest wavelength and hence the highest $n$ in a dispersive medium, so its critical angle is the smallest.
questions.trick: Critical angle: $\sin C=1/n$ — higher $n$ (violet) gives smaller critical angle, always.

questions.q: The relation $f = R/2$ between the focal length and radius of curvature of a spherical mirror is strictly valid only for
options: marginal rays incident at a large aperture
paraxial rays making small angles with the principal axis
convex mirrors only, not concave mirrors
rays that are parallel to the principal axis at any height
questions.explanation: The relation $f=R/2$ follows from the small-angle (paraxial) approximation. For marginal rays striking near the edge of a large-aperture mirror, this relation fails, causing spherical aberration.
questions.trick: $f=R/2$ holds only for paraxial rays; marginal rays cause spherical aberration.

questions.q: A biconvex lens of focal length 15 cm is cut into two identical halves by a plane containing the principal axis (sliced from top to bottom). The focal length of each half is
questions.explanation: Cutting along a plane containing the principal axis only reduces the aperture (making the image dimmer); the radii of curvature of each half are unchanged, so each half still has focal length 15 cm.
questions.trick: Cutting along the axis only reduces aperture — focal length of each half stays $f$.

questions.q: In an astronomical telescope in normal adjustment, the final image formed is
options: real, inverted, diminished, at the eyepiece's focus
real, erect and of the same size
virtual, inverted and formed at infinity
questions.explanation: In normal adjustment, the objective's real image falls at the eyepiece's focus, and the eyepiece then forms the final image at infinity; it remains virtual and inverted with respect to the object.
questions.trick: Astronomical telescope, normal adjustment: final image is virtual, inverted, at infinity.

questions.q: In a compound microscope, the image formed by the objective lens (which then acts as the object for the eyepiece) is
options: real, erect and of the same size
questions.explanation: The object is placed just beyond the objective's focal length, so the objective forms a real, inverted, magnified image, which the eyepiece then further magnifies as a simple microscope.
questions.trick: Objective of compound microscope always forms a real, inverted, magnified image first.

questions.q: A ray of light enters perpendicular to one face of a 45°-45°-90° glass prism ($n=1.5$) and strikes the hypotenuse face at 45°, which exceeds the critical angle (about 41.8°), so it undergoes total internal reflection and emerges perpendicular to the other short face. The ray has been turned through
questions.explanation: The single total internal reflection at the hypotenuse bends the ray by 90°, which is why such prisms are used in binoculars and periscopes instead of mirrors.
questions.trick: 45-45-90 TIR prism: light undergoes total internal reflection and turns exactly 90°.

questions.q: An equiconvex lens of glass ($n=1.5$) has a certain focal length in air. When it is completely immersed in water ($n=4/3$), the percentage increase in its focal length is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{f_w}{f_a}=\dfrac{n_g-1}{n_g/n_w-1}=\dfrac{0.5}{1.125-1}=4$, so the focal length becomes 4 times its original value — an increase of $(4-1)\times100\% = 300\%$.
questions.trick: Lens in water: focal length becomes 4$\times$ for $n=1.5$ glass — a 300% rise.

questions.q: A ray of light passes symmetrically through an equilateral glass prism (angle of prism $A=60^\circ$) such that the angle of incidence equals the angle of emergence, each equal to $\dfrac34$ of the angle of the prism. The angle of deviation is
questions.explanation: $i=e=\dfrac34\times60^\circ=45^\circ$. Deviation $\delta=i+e-A=45+45-60=30^\circ$.
questions.trick: Prism deviation: $\delta=i+e-A$ — plug in the given $i$ and $e$ directly.

questions.q: In an experiment to find the focal length of a convex lens by the displacement method, the distance between the object and the screen is fixed at 90 cm. Two positions of the lens, 30 cm apart, both give a sharp image on the screen. The focal length of the lens is
questions.explanation: By the displacement (Bessel's) method, $f=\dfrac{D^2-d^2}{4D}=\dfrac{90^2-30^2}{4\times90}=\dfrac{7200}{360}=20$ cm.
questions.trick: Displacement method: $f=(D^2-d^2)/(4D)$ using object-screen distance $D$ and shift $d$.

questions.q: An equi-concave lens made of glass ($n=1.5$) has a power of $-5$ D. The magnitude of the radius of curvature of each surface is
questions.explanation: $|f|=1/|P|=1/5$ m $=20$ cm. For an equi-concave lens, $\left|\dfrac1f\right|=(n-1)\dfrac2R \Rightarrow \dfrac1{20}=0.5\times\dfrac2R \Rightarrow R=20$ cm.
questions.trick: Equi-concave: $|1/f|=(n-1)(2/R)$ — solve for $R$ from the given power.

questions.q: Two thin convex and concave lenses are placed in contact to form an achromatic combination. If both lenses are made of the same material (same dispersive power), then
options: the combination is impossible only if the focal lengths differ
the two focal lengths must be equal and of the same sign, doubling the power
the two focal lengths must be equal in magnitude but opposite in sign, so the net power is zero
achromatism needs unequal dispersive powers, so any pair of focal lengths works here
questions.explanation: Achromatism requires $\dfrac{\omega_1}{f_1}+\dfrac{\omega_2}{f_2}=0$. If $\omega_1=\omega_2$ (same material), this forces $f_1=-f_2$, so the net power $1/f_1+1/f_2=0$ — the combination has no focusing ability, making it useless despite being achromatic.
questions.trick: Achromatic pair needs different materials; same material forces $f_1=-f_2$, net power zero.

questions.q: An ink dot is viewed from directly above through a travelling microscope. When a glass slab of thickness 6 cm is placed over the dot, it appears to rise (shift upward) by 2 cm. The refractive index of the glass is
questions.explanation: Apparent shift $=t\left(1-\dfrac1n\right)$. So $2=6\left(1-\dfrac1n\right) \Rightarrow 1-\dfrac1n=\dfrac13 \Rightarrow \dfrac1n=\dfrac23 \Rightarrow n=1.5$.
questions.trick: Apparent rise through slab: shift $=t(1-1/n)$ — solve for $n$ directly.

questions.q: In a primary rainbow, the colours violet and red appear
options: with violet on the inner edge of the arc and red on the outer edge
with red on the inner edge of the arc and violet on the outer edge
with violet on top and red at the bottom of the arc
at the same position, since both deviate equally
questions.explanation: Violet light emerges from raindrops at a smaller angle from the direction of sunlight than red, so violet appears on the inner edge and red on the outer edge of a primary rainbow.
questions.trick: Primary rainbow: violet deviates most, so it appears on the inner arc.

questions.q: The objective lens of a telescope has a diameter of 10 cm. For light of wavelength 550 nm, the telescope's limit of resolution (minimum resolvable angular separation) is approximately
questions.explanation: Limit of resolution $\Delta\theta = \dfrac{1.22\lambda}{D} = \dfrac{1.22\times550\times10^{-9}}{0.10} \approx 6.7\times10^{-6}$ rad.
questions.trick: Telescope resolving power: $\Delta\theta=1.22\lambda/D$ — smaller angle means finer resolution.

questions.q: The critical angle for light travelling from glass ($n=1.5$) into water ($n=4/3$) is
questions.explanation: For denser (glass) to rarer (water), $\sin C = \dfrac{n_{water}}{n_{glass}} = \dfrac{4/3}{1.5} = \dfrac89 \approx 0.889 \Rightarrow C \approx 62.7^\circ$.
questions.trick: Denser-to-rarer critical angle: $\sin C = n(\text{rarer})/n(\text{denser})$ — glass to water here.

questions.q: For an equilateral prism ($A=60^\circ$), the angle of minimum deviation happens to equal the angle of the prism itself ($\delta_m = A = 60^\circ$). The speed of light inside this prism is
questions.explanation: $n=\dfrac{\sin\frac{A+\delta_m}{2}}{\sin\frac A2}=\dfrac{\sin60^\circ}{\sin30^\circ}=\dfrac{0.866}{0.5}=\sqrt3$. So $v=c/n=3\times10^8/\sqrt3\approx1.73\times10^8$ m/s.
questions.trick: Special case $\delta_m=A$: $n=2\cos(A/2)$ — then find $v=c/n$ directly.

questions.q: A symmetric biconvex lens of focal length 15 cm is cut by a plane perpendicular to the principal axis, through its optical centre, giving two plano-convex halves. The focal length of each half is
questions.explanation: Cutting perpendicular to the axis gives each half only one curved surface instead of two, halving its power; since power is halved, the focal length doubles: $2\times15=30$ cm.
questions.trick: Perpendicular cut splits a symmetric biconvex lens into two lenses of focal length $2f$ each.

questions.q: A point object moves with a constant speed of 2 m/s along the principal axis, towards a convex lens of focal length 10 cm, and is instantaneously at a distance of 15 cm from the lens. The speed of the image at this instant is
questions.explanation: At $u=-15$ cm, $\dfrac1v=\dfrac1{10}-\dfrac1{15}=\dfrac1{30}\Rightarrow v=30$ cm, so $m=v/u=-2$. Since $\left|\dfrac{dv}{dt}\right|=m^2\left|\dfrac{du}{dt}\right|=4\times2=8$ m/s.
questions.trick: Image speed $= m^2 \times$ object speed, using $m=v/u$ at that instant.

questions.q: A plano-convex lens (focal length 20 cm as a lens, $n=1.5$) has its curved surface silvered instead of its plane surface. The equivalent focal length of this mirror-like system is
questions.explanation: For a plano-convex lens, $\dfrac1{f_{lens}}=\dfrac{n-1}{R}$, so with $f_{lens}=20$ cm, $R=(n-1)\times20=10$ cm. Silvering the curved surface gives a mirror of power $P_{mirror}=\dfrac2R=0.2\,\text{cm}^{-1}$, while $P_{lens}=\dfrac1{20}=0.05\,\text{cm}^{-1}$. Equivalent power $P_{eq}=2P_{lens}+P_{mirror}=0.1+0.2=0.3\,\text{cm}^{-1}$, giving $F_{eq}=1/0.3\approx3.33$ cm.
questions.trick: Curved surface silvered: $P_{eq}=2P_{lens}+2/R$, not the plane-silvered formula — don't mix them up.

questions.q: A thin prism of angle $6^\circ$ is made of a material with refractive indices $n_v=1.532$ for violet and $n_r=1.514$ for red light. The angular dispersion produced between violet and red is
questions.explanation: Angular dispersion $=(n_v-n_r)A=(1.532-1.514)\times6^\circ=0.018\times6^\circ=0.108^\circ$.
questions.trick: Angular dispersion of a thin prism $=(n_v-n_r)\times A$ — a direct product.
